utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. And for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the learned colleagues from the OTP, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with Lejla Gluhic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me just remind you, sir, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I hope you are rested and we can continue today.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to be shown PT1673.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is bulletin number 5, dated the 6th of January, 1994, which you commented upon in paragraph 65 of your statement. You said that since the document does not bear a stamp, most probably it was a draft version of the document. Nevertheless, I should like you to look at the contents of it, since it was admitted into evidence. Can you turn to page 4 of the document, please, or, rather, page 3 of the Bosnian version and page 4 of the English. Page 3 of the Bosnian. Witness, please -- or, rather, let us look at the next page of the Bosnian version. The English version is fine. Thank you. Can we see the entire paragraph? Yes, thank you. Witness, please take a look at the paragraph, and you will see that this is a report where a man called "Abu Muhamed El Kasim," a fighter of the El Mujahedin unit, had sent two letters to Saudi Arabia. In one of the letters, he informs them that he had become -- that he is on very good terms with the Supreme Command, who blindly trust him?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following: The Supreme Command is not the General Staff, is it; "the Supreme Command" is a broader term, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command is the Presidency, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following in relation to this document: You worked as the head of the Analysis Department of the Military Security Administration, and you handled hundreds of such reports which concerned Arabs, the El Mujahedin Detachment, and their connections. Please, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber and can you recall whether you had ever seen a single report pointing to a link between General Delic -- a direct link between him and members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is characteristic, since he was the commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command, and as such you would probably have recalled or remembered that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document or Exhibit 742, and can we put this document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the document. For the transcript, this is Special Information Report number 87, dated the 16th of August, 1995. Apparently, Witness -- or, rather, please look at the signature at the top. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These are my initials, and I wrote the date, the "16th of August."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can the witness be shown page 2, please. Let's turn to page 2 of the document, and I believe it's page 2 in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're the author of this document, I presume, depending on the basis of the initials, or at least you saw it, and the document speaks of the disrupted, troubled relations between the Command of the 35th Division and the civilian authorities of Zavidovici Municipality. Please go through the document, and then I'll ask you a question about its contents. It follows from the document that the political structures of Zavidovici demanded that they be submitted reports on all the activities and plans for combat activities within the municipality, and generally the document speaks of the close relations that exist between the Zavidovici Municipality and the El Mujahedin Detachment and the Company of Asim Camdzic; is it right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Analysing the information you received, you would also receive information such as this one about the interference of the municipality authorities in Bosnian -- or, rather, of the interference of Bosnian municipality -- municipal authorities into municipal matters?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several such cases.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Madam Vidovic please repeat her question? The interpreter isn't sure that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's asked that you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following. I will repeat the question, Your Honours, because it doesn't reflect what I said. Witness, I said the following: In performing your work in the Analysis Department, you received information about the interference on the part of the civilian authorities into military matters within the municipalities of Central Bosnia? This was my question. Do you recall? Can you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to this particular case, there were several others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall which were the municipalities in question?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, I can definitely recall that there was one such case in the territory of Konjic Municipality. I believe there was one such case in the area of Zenica Municipality or that's to say in Zenica proper, and of course in other municipalities, but I can't recall them at present, but there were such cases, for sure. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, we can put this document away. It's already been admitted into evidence. I want the witness to be shown a different document. Can the witness be shown P1937. This is bulletin number 9, dated the 13th of January, 1995. This is one of the bulletins which you said in your statement you recognised. Can the witness be shown page 3 of the document, please. Until we get the English version, please read paragraph 2 concerning the 3rd Corps. I will ask you something about the principle of work in dealing with documents such as this one. The first portion of the document will suffice. I would like the Trial Chamber to see the document. Can you please scroll down, once we finish reading the paragraph, because we can only see half of the paragraph in the English version, Your Honours. The other half is on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you've read this, Witness. From this portion of the bulletin, one could conclude, could we not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Really. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From this portion of the bulletin, one could conclude, could one not, that Abu Maali had said that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina could give its authorisation for the entry of 50 Afghans into Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the government can give that authorisation. This is something that the reader of this passage would conclude?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please keep this piece of information in mind. Can this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours, please, and can it be put away, because I wish to show the witness another document which is connected to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 680. 680. Page 3 of the Bosnian version and 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can see that this is an official note of the Ministry of the Interior concerning the reproductions of wire-tapped conversations. Can we look at reproduction number 42. It is in the middle of the page. Can we zoom in on paragraph 42, please. These are the contents of the wire-tapped conversations, intercepted conversations of the 6th of January, 1995. It is stated: "Abdurahman informs Meali that through the Turkish organisation, IMH, 50 Afghans have arrived in Turkey, and asks Meali whether he can get permission from the BH Government for them coming to Bosnia, to which Meali replies that they should not go through official channels because they are able to transfer them." You will agree, Witness, will you not, that this is the original information on the basis of which that other report was made, the one -- or that other information was written that we saw in Exhibit 763, where it was roughly said that the government can make this possible. Do you agree, Witness, that the content of the information we have here is, in fact, quite different. Maali suggested here that they should not go through the official channels of the government because they were able to take care of the transfer of the Afghans themselves. Let me ask you this in connection with that: Would you agree with me that the person writing the bulletin must have interpreted the same piece of information differently, in a different way than it was, in fact, written here?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Errors in the process of conveying information in the form of bulletins were quite possible, they could happen quite possibly, could they not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put this document away, please. On the topic of including information into bulletins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, before we put this document back into the computer, I'd like to ask you what it really is that you are seeking to show here. Is it that the same piece of information was interpreted differently by two members of the witness's team or is it to show that, in fact, in the end those extra Arabs who were to come did not arrive into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the official channels, but came in an informal way and were introduced by already-existing members of the El Mujahid in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm unsure of what it is you want to elicit from this witness in relation to these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to elicit from the witness the former, what you said before. The information -- the report we have before us is the information from the Military Security Service which intercepted the information, which was subsequently misinterpreted in the bulletin. What I want to say is that the information contained in the bulletins may be inaccurate because they were misinterpreted in the process of being made, the information was misinterpreted in the process of making the bulletins, and I want to show the degree to which these bulletins are, in fact, accurate and reliable. I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You were indeed. So just to confirm that, your point is to confirm the information that we see in the bulletins may not always be reliable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to show the witness Exhibit 736. And can we put this document away, please. This is bulletin number 125 from the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You referred to this bulletin in paragraph 47 of your statement. May we show the last paragraph of page 5 of the document, please. Before the English version appears on the screen, please take a look at the text starting with: "The Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps." That's the following page on the English. This is okay now. I draw your attention to the section which mentions the 3rd Corps. Let me quote a fraction of that. It reads: "The Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps reports that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, while on the Ozren-Vozuca front, frequently visited soldiers of the adjacent unit, the 328th Brigade, and threatened them, especially the Croatian and Serbian soldiers." And then further on it says that they asked for one of its soldiers, who is a Croat, saying that they would slaughter all Croats and Chetniks. Do you agree that the gist of this part of the bulletin is that the El Mujahedin threatened all Croats and Chetniks with slaughter, those members of the 328th Brigade, so this is the gist of this information; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I go to another document which is connected with this, please tell me whether you agree that at the end it is stated, just as in other bulletins, that the Military Security Service, in coordination with the organs of command and control, is taking steps to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you agree that you -- not you, personally, but your department prepared such information on the basis of raw information that you received from your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this can be clearly seen in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Can we put this document away, please. And may we show the witness D586, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see the pseudonym "White Chicken" or "Bijela Koka." Please look at the seal or stamp on this page. Can you confirm this is the document by the 3rd Corps Command, the Department of Military Security, dated the 7th [Realtime transcript read in error "17"] of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we scroll up to the text, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Military Security Service kept their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the 7th of July the date of this document or --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is the 7th of July, as I said, the 7th of July. It was entered in the transcript wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So can we go back to the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm going to ask you again: Do you agree that members of the Military Security Service maintained their sources and their associates covered under pseudonym or code names?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree this was their duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now please read -- I see that you were looking at the text. Could you read it? And there is a sentence which begins with the course of -- "This is what happened ..." This would be towards the middle, Your Honours, starting with: "This is what happened ..." Witness, please take a look at this. It reads: "This is what happened:" They are referring to Miro Huncek. This is the person referred to in the bulletin that we just saw. It reads: "As soon as they arrived, they asked for a member of a unit of the 1st Battalion with these words: 'Where is Mira Huncek?' The platoon commander answered there was no Miro, only Mihro. And this is what he said, that: 'We had no Mihro, but Miro, the Croat. I want to slit his throat.' Throughout this time, Mira Huncek was nearby, observing what was happening. The platoon commander managed to wink at Huncek, indicating that he wanted him to leave the grounds of the company command, which Huncek did." And the next sentence is: "The news spread along the line of defence that members of the El Mujahedin unit were coming, wanted to slaughter all non-Muslim members." After that: "After these events, rumours started to spread through the town that there was no point in the Croats and the remaining Serbs going to the line of defence because members of the El Mujahedin would apparently slaughter them, be they on the line or at home." Witness, in connection with this, I would like to ask you this: You just saw that the gist of this information that was introduced into the bulletin -- into the bulletin which was Exhibit 736, so the gist of that information was the El Mujahedin Detachment members are visiting the line of defence, threatening to slaughter all Croats and Serbs. You would agree that this document is the raw or original document used for the preparation of the bulletin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the primary or raw document which is being exaggerated maybe by somebody at the 3rd Corps Security Service Department or at the -- our administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this rumour which is mentioned in the raw document entered into the bulletin; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apparently it entered the bulletin as correct, accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it's clearly shown in this document that rumours concerning the El Mujahedin can be overblown and they can reach such a high level as your bulletin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a frequent occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, may this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before, what is actually the rumour here that is spreading? I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this can be seen from the text of this information that rumours were relayed from the line of defence into town centre that the El Mujahedin were about to slaughter all Serbs and Croats, be they on the line of defence or be they at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it a rumour or was it something that was quoted -- that is put into quotes in the previous document, where it says: "I want to slit the throats of all Chetniks and Serbs," or whatever it said? I can't remember. That was a quotation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, this was a quote, but I cannot be precise about it, whether it was a misinterpretation on the part of the 3rd Corps analyst or an analyst in the Military Security Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's for you to determine. How would you know? You're receiving a quote. A quote is a quote is a quote. It cannot be a rumour. You can't expect that which is in quotation marks to be misinterpreted, because the person who's writing that is saying, "Lest I misinterpret, I'll tell you exactly what was said, so it's for you, the reader, to interpret what that means." So you can't then say the 3rd Corps misinterpreted it if they quoted it. So I want to know what the rumour is here you're talking about, that you're agreeing to that was spread, because this document says the news spread along the company command, along the line of defence. That is the news, not the rumour. The news, that is in quotes. Okay, you're not able to tell us what the rumour is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I clarify one thing? In this case, it goes for a raw document prepared by an operative out in the field. This document was processed in the Military Security Department of the 3rd Corps, and most probably the analysts of the 3rd Corps in question wrote the section as presented in the "Biltin" -- or rather as written in his daily report as sent to the Military Security Administration of the Supreme Command Staff. Therefore, a mistake occurred in the Military Security Department of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I believe that the interpretation is wrong again. The person that is interpreting is interpreting construing what the witness is saying and not translating what he is saying. I don't know why this is happening, Your Honours. I would like this to enter into the transcript. The witness specifically says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just stop testifying. Let's ask the interpreters to interpret. Say what you wanted to say and let the interpreters interpret again. And then if they still misinterpret, Madam Vidovic, tell us where you say they misinterpret and let's go back to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm exactly referring to what the witness already said. The witness says this is a primary document, and this is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is not reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not enter into the transcript in the first sentence of his reply in line 14 on page 15, that the witness referred to a primary document, and this is why you cannot understand what is being discussed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you and the witness have been using the word "raw" and "primary" interchangeably, and at line 14, yes, the word "primary" is not there, but the word "raw" is there. It doesn't help, Madam Vidovic, to be -- to look exasperated. All I want to understand is what is the rumour. You're taking me all over this document, and you're not -- I'm not getting an answer to my question. What was the rumour that was being propagated? I don't care whether it's a primary document or not a primary document. That's all I want to know. And it doesn't help to say, "Aah."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not for a single moment did I use the word, in Bosnian, "raw." Neither did the witness. What is entered into the transcript are replies and -- permit me to finish, Your Honours. We cannot understand one another, neither you, I or the witness, if I say "primary" and the witness says "primary," it is interpreted as "raw," then you cannot receive the witness's reply. And allow me, Your Honours, to say that this creates grave problems in our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now understand one thing. I don't understand a word of B/C/S, so when you speak and the interpreters say "raw" at some stage and at some stage they say "primary," I say, "Okay, that's how you interchange the words." And if nobody, when the word is first misused, doesn't say, "Sorry, I didn't say 'raw', I said 'primary'," then I accept that you're using the words interchangeably. But again I go back to my point. That's not the point I'm raising. I'm asking what is the rumour that was being spread, irrespective of whether that rumour comes from a raw or a primary statement? All I want to know is what is the rumour, and let's concentrate on that and forget about "raw" and "primary." Yeah. What is the rumour?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not being able to -- he agreed with you that a rumour spread, and I stopped, I said, "Wait a minute, what is the rumour?" And in all his answers, I have not been told what the rumour is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like the witness to answer me at this point. I would like to know, sir, what is the rumour that was spreading? And don't tell me about where things came from, just tell me, what is the rumour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it can be seen in the text. The rumours referred to members of El Mujahedin Detachment threatening to slit the throats of remaining Serbs and Croats, be they at home or at the line of defence. These were the rumours. This was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You already showed me that text, but the rumour --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me assist. In the English text, it starts with the words: "After these events ..." That's toward the end of this large paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The rumour there says that there was no point in the Croats and the remaining Serbs going to the line of defence, not that the El Mujahedin wants to slit -- kill everybody. That's not the rumour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the sentence that precedes this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That precedes this one: "The news spread along the line of defence that members of the El Mujahid unit were coming, wanting to slaughter all non-Muslims." But that's what they said in the quote that I referred to. That's what they said, they wanted to kill them. So this is not an incorrect report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may put a question to the witness, Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this primary document you have before you speaks, in fact, about a Mujahedin threatening a man by the name of Mira Huncek, so this was one member of that unit threatening one person, Mira Huncek; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And right after that, the document states that the news spread along the line of defence that members of the El Mujahedin unit were touring the area with the intention of slaughtering them, so it was on the basis of this one incident, involving one individual, that the rumours spread? Am I interpreting this document correctly?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me go back to that bulletin. This expanded form of this piece of information was, in fact, entered into the bulletin that we saw. Can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The bulletin does not state that this was a rumour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And one can see from this document that it was indeed a rumour, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we put this document away -- or, rather, can we have it admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 764.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness look at Exhibit 711 now. As you can see, this is Special Information Report number 12, dated the 2nd of April, 1993. This was among the documents the authenticity of which you confirmed yesterday. Can we turn to page 2 of the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document is entitled "Information on the Inappropriate Behaviour of Rasim Delic." Witness, please look at the second paragraph of the document. Before that, can the witness be shown the signature, the name and surname of the author of the document. Do you agree with me that it says "Chief Fikret Muslimovic"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recognise his signature? Is this his signature?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the paragraph starting with: "According to ..." Do you agree that the Chief Fikret Muslimovic speaks of the information he received about the fact that Rasim Delic was assigned a flat, his disinterestedness about what was going on in combat activities, his presence in cafes and hotels? Please keep this information in mind, because I will be showing you other documents on this issue. You had worked with General Delic and you knew him personally, and you knew a great deal about him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we put this document away now. Can the witness be shown Exhibit 210 now. Since this is a document under seal, can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D642. This is page 1 -- or, rather, the cover page of Fikret Muslimovic's book called "Arguments and Memories of War (1990-1993)."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the one-and-only Fikret Muslimovic who was in the General Staff, was he not, and who worked in the Security Administration and later on as the Chief of the Administration for Moral Guidance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. Please look at the passage entitled "About BH Army Personnel." I will quote fractions of this passage: "President Izetbegovic then inquired about personnel within the RBiH Army. He asked who former JNA officers were who could be counted on to perform highest functions in RBiH Army. I said that there were few Bosniak officers in the JNA who held high ranks and who had experience in performing of high military functions." I will be skipping about now, Witness, to save time. Further down, the text reads: "I said that Delic was in Visoko ..." This is somewhere in the middle of the document: "I said that Rasim Delic, who had left the JNA with the rank of lieutenant colonel, at the start of the aggression. Since I know him well, since we graduated from the Military Academy together, the Land Artillery Department, I gave very positive evaluations of him. I pointed out that Delic was extremely -- a person of moral integrity and great discipline and that he was committed to his family and official obligations. I assessed that he was adequate for the most significant duties in the RBiH Army, that's to say that he belonged in the Supreme Command Staff on one of the highest-level positions." Do you agree with me, Witness, that in this book which General Muslimovic obviously wrote after the war, he gave a completely different piece of information about General Delic, compared to the one that he had written in that special information report; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Back there, he described him as an immoral person and here as a moral -- as a highly moral person?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Muslimovic was the Chief of the Counter-Intelligence Department of the 7th Army District before the war, and therefore I'm referring to the JNA. As a JNA officer, he had different criteria from mine. I often opposed his method of reporting because he did not -- was non-critical. What I want to say is that he should not have, because it was not the practice of the Security Administrations to inform the top military and state leadership on the basis of a single piece of information. The information had to be double-checked and verified, and if it came from only one source, then it -- one had to indicate that it came from only one source. I have just recalled one such case. At the start of the war, I was writing a report for the President of the War Presidency of Gorazde which was highly negative. It involved one source, and I contradicted him, and I told him that something like that should not be written about the President Izetbegovic, since the information only came from one source. I told him that of course should we receive further information to that effect about the President of the Presidency, then we could compare it with other sources and see how accurate the information was. However, he insisted that I write that down, to write down the gist of the information. Since it was late at night, I didn't get any sleep that night. I was going through this internal struggle, asking myself whether I should write such information about a person, information which I wasn't sure was true, but I did it ultimately because I was ordered by him to do this. He had these very rigid positions which were quite -- which lacked critical perspective. Now that I see who the author of this report on General Delic is, it's Rusim Sejdinovic -- Husnija Sejdinovic, and since he was an experienced analyst, I'm really wondering at him writing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally knew General Delic. Would you accept as accurate in any way that piece of information which Fikret Muslimovic wrote originally, the author of which is Mr. Sejdinovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can this excerpt from General Muslimovic's book be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: D642 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 765.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness look at document 643 briefly. D643. Witness, you can see that this is the Special Information Report number 243. I would like the witness to look at the last page of the document to see his initials and confirm that these are his initials on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that these are your initials?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 of the document, please, or, rather, page 2. Page 2. Please read the first part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the document is entitled: "Obstruction of work by certain members of the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document says that the Military Security Department of the 3rd Corps had problems and disputes arising between Mr. Dugalic and certain members of the Military Security Sector of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had information and knowledge about these problems, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It seemed that Commander Dugalic wanted discipline to reign, and that in connection with this there was some obstructions and some problems arising; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document into evidence, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, put this document away, and please show the witness document P1556. This is yet another Special Information Report number 189, dated 24th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were still an analyst in this department, in this part of the administration which produced such special information reports?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we first turn to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you recognise this signature.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Chief Jusuf Jasarevic, and the initials of Husnija Sejdinovic that you mentioned a couple of times?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's go to page 2 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Witness, that this document discusses some security-related actions of the deputy commander of the General Staff during the execution of his duty at the IKM Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, then, that the Military Security Service was engaged in counter-intelligence protection and subjected and targeted the commander -- personnel of the Army of BiH to questioning?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their conduct was being monitored?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we just saw that Military Security Service monitored the conduct of their own leaders?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document into evidence, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we show D640 to the witness, please. This is an information concerning negative reporting in some media, dated 24th of September, 1996, addressed to the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Madam Vidovic. I note that the English version says "1995" instead of "1996", on the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995. I erred. The original refers to 1995. This is -- the last digit is "5", and it would be evident from the contents. Now can we turn to page 2 -- or, rather, page 3 of the document. That would be page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the time, mid-September 1995, you worked at the Supreme Command Staff, did you not? Now I would like you to read this paragraph which discusses -- and I can quote it, and that would be the last paragraph in the English version. Could this be zoomed in on or can the English version be scrolled down, please, so that the last paragraph is visible. Witness, please, this document discusses that the authority of the commander of the General Staff, Army General Rasim Delic, is being exposed to open irony in the "Masala Dzoka" [phoen] article authored by Sead Fetahagic published in the "Oslobodjenje" on the 18th September 1995, and similarly in an article entitled "51 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina liberated," by Senad Avdic, in "Slobodna Bosna", Issue 2 of the 21st of September 1995, and through inappropriate comparison quotes: "Dudakovic almost in Banja Luka, Delic almost in Kuala Lumpur," and that by doing so, they erroneously represented the activities of the purposes concerned: Witness, you worked in September 1995 in General Supreme Staff -- in the General Staff, your administration and the Moral Guidance Administration were involved in media and publicity. It is true, is it not, that in September 1995 there were a slough of attacks against General Delic for his -- at the time when the fighting going on, for his being at Malaysia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember these -- this coverage of these articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is why we have this ironic title, "Dudakovic almost in Banja Luka," who is the Chief of the 5th Corps: "Dukekovic almost in Banja Luka, Delic almost in Kula Lumpur"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours, and maybe I have a couple of minutes more to finish after the break, after the break, Your Honours. I believe that this is the right time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, but you realise, Madam Vidovic, that from yesterday when you said you would be an hour, you've already taken more than one and a half hours, taken -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've taken three hours and 15 minutes to date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, Your Honours. But believe me that I did my best to go through the huge number of documents admitted by the Prosecutor in the simplest of ways, without neglecting my duty towards my clients in this case and in another case. I will be in a position, by leave, to use quite a lot of time in my cross when it comes to the witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter, because there is no other way -- if there are hundreds of documents being admitted, I would be failing in my duty if I were not to confront the witness with what I have to confront him or her with. And I truly believe it will take me no more than five or six minutes after the break, and this is what I'm duty-bound to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I will repeat what I told you when those documents were admitted, that they were not admitted for the truthfulness of their contents, so that in fact whether or not their contents is truthful is not going to be material in this case. So I'm not quite sure what is the purpose of this cross-examination. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right to say that document 640 has not been tendered yet -- has been tendered but has not been given an exhibit number? Okay. It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit 768.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to ask you briefly about a portion of your statement which concerns the morning briefings of the Military Security Administration that you described in paragraph 21 of your statement. You remember discussing that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that special attention was paid by the administration to training and that this was something very frequently discussed at briefings, but all other issues, important issues, were discussed as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May D641 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Witness, Mr. Vuckovic, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. This is my -- this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we show the next page of this document to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here I would like to show you some portions of this document. Please pay attention to the day the 8th of August, 1994. Please take a look at paragraphs 1 and 6 of this document. Paragraphs 1 and 6. Please read them to yourself. This is your handwriting. And after that I'm going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the handwriting. This is Husnija Sejdinovic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I thought it was yours. I apologise. You will agree with me that in these paragraphs, it is stated that the Military Security Service, in conducting operative activities, encountered a number of objective difficulties or obstructions in its work. Do you agree that, as an example, that the Trebevic-4 operation was cited?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, "4" or "2"? The interpreter says "4", the document says "2", at least the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please take a look at paragraph 1 on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to this. So at this point, I was discussing this point, but in paragraph 6 it makes reference to what His Honour Moloto said, that there are obstructions in the criminal proceedings or trials with the framework of T-2 operation and that organs -- [indiscernible] held a meeting there about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at page 3 of the document now. The problems that we saw discussed there, Military Security Service encountered obstruction within its own ranks and obstructions within the judicial system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look, on page 3, minutes of meetings of the briefing of the 6th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please read the first three sentences on this page. Do you agree that at the Collegium of the Military Security Service, what was highlighted was the need to use that service to collect documents for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was stated that the Prosecutor from the International Court in The Hague came to Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And your service, in connection with this, adopts a conclusion that war crime cases should be worked on. What I'd like to ask you about this, the war crimes issues, is: Do you agree that the Army of BiH General Staff immediately, on the 6th of September, immediately after the Prosecutor came, accepted to work with the International Criminal Tribunal's Prosecutors; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I clearly know that because I was the one to assess the collected documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were already working, following instructions of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That cooperation, Mr. Vuckovic, was accepted, among other things, because that was the position of General Delic with regard to war crimes, that cooperation must be started with the International Criminal Tribunal's Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Army of BiH opened all its archives, including the General Staff's president's archives and made them available to the Prosecutor; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right in saying so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As early as 1995, at the request of the Prosecutor, the Government of BiH extradited members of the Army of BiH, gentlemen Lanco [phoen] and Delic to be tried here at the Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before, only one person had been indicted here before them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So trials started here at the Tribunal, trying the Muslims or Bosniaks, because it was the position of the Supreme Command Staff was that they should be tried; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions. But before, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have just a single question, I think. Your testimony here before us, sir, has been mainly to establish that the information was passed on to the General Staff. Now, you may have noticed that there has been some uncertainty as to the truthfulness of the contents of the reports that were passed on to the General Staff. But be that as it may, my question to you would be if you could provide us with some information as to your knowledge of whether General Delic actually received these reports and had a chance to familiarise himself with the contents. In other words, was he put on notice about the activities of the El Mujahid Detachment and the other Mujahedin groups that were contained in your reports? That's the crucial issue in relation to your testimony. Can you help us out?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my main task was to assess the information received from the corps level and other sources of information, also the information received on the basis of cooperation with other security services such as the State Security Service, Military Intelligence Service. On the basis of these, my assessments, and on the basis of the assessments of General Jasarevic, the head of the Military Security Administration, together with our team of analysts, we prepared these reports for which we believed that -- which we believed that the army general -- that the army commander, General Delic, and President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic as the Commander-in-Chief, the Prime Minister, Ministry of Defence, sometimes the Minister of Foreign Affairs if there were matters lying within his competence, would keep them informed on various activities such as the counter-intelligence activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance. We did this job of ours conscientiously and responsibly, and the reports drafted in my department would be ultimately verified by General Jasarevic, as the head of the administration. And the reports would, of course, be dispatched to the recipients. Therefore, my task was to make sure that the reports were as concise and brief as possible, whilst containing the gist of these matters. The procedure that followed was not of any interest to me in those times of war, and I'm referring to the ways in which the reports would be sent from there and what would happen with them. That was the matter for General Jasarevic. What I thought was important was to make sure that the daily bulletin was finished and ready by 12.00 midday, and that's why I controlled my analysts to see whether they were lagging behind in preparing bulletins, special information reports, sometimes in making assessments, overviews and so on and so forth. I was monitoring their work in order to make sure that it was done in a timely fashion. I did not have any further obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure you did a good job, and I am not putting that into question. Do you recall any times when, for instance, General Delic or someone from the General Staff would come back to you and react upon your bulletins and your reports? In other words, did you have any impression or knowledge about whether they actually read those reports and took actions, relevant actions?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already mentioned this in my evidence, in my statement. I do remember that on several occasions Mr. Delic made some annotations to the effect that we should keep up the work that we were doing, or when an operative task was completed, he would make a note saying that the job was well done. These annotations of his, of course, served as encouragement for me and my colleagues in our future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in short, you were convinced that General Delic and his immediate staff actually did read your reports and did take whatever actions they thought was necessary?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL VUCKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wrote the reports with the intention of them reaching the readers and intending for them to be read by them. Whether they indeed read the reports and when, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the Judge's questions, starting with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vuckovic, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Let's take this time to thank you very much for taking the time out of your busy schedule to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down, and please do travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May the witness please make the declaration. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. And good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Spahic, could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: My name is Salih Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And could you please state your date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of May, 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And your place of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And just for the record, in which country is Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, did you provide a written statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in September of 2006, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And at the time that you provided that written statement, sir, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I answered the questions of that investigator truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you answer the questions freely, sir, and that's without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I answered the questions freely, without any coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that interview, sir, was your statement read back to you in the Bosnian language, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the conclusion of that interview, the translation was -- or rather it was read to me in the Serbian language, translated back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And did you then sign that statement in the English language, sir, the English language version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P06198, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While the exhibit is coming: Sir, you didn't sign the B/C/S statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't sign the statement in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down on the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, you have now before you both the Bosnian and the English versions of your statement. Do you see your signature on the English version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived here earlier this week, in preparation for your testimony, were you given an opportunity to review the version of this statement which is in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. On my arrival in The Hague, I had the opportunity to see the Bosnian version of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you review that version of your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And after you finished reviewing your statement, were you given an opportunity to make any corrections that you desired to your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P06207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what will the Court do with P06198?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the document that I'm going to be showing the witness is actually the corrections that he made, so once he adopts that, I would just ask that both the statement that's on the screen now and his corrections be admitted as a single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "MS. VIDOVIC"] 6207, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 6207. Sorry, there's a lot of things. Madam Vidovic's name is being mentioned here, and she's been quiet all this afternoon. I don't know why she's being mentioned on the record, and figures that have been not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I think they put Madam Vidovic's name where my name should have appeared, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Do you want to swap places?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm actually pretty comfortable here, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, does the document in front of you list the corrections that you made to your statement? Sir? Let me repeat the question. Does the document in front of you list the corrections that you made to your statement? I'm not sure if the translation is going through, but the witness doesn't seem to be -- Mr. Spahic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like he's still reading --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to check whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Spahic. Now, if we could go to page 8 of the Bosnian version and page 7 of the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see -- do you see your signature on the Bosnian version of this document?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I were to ask you -- if questions were to be put to you during the course of your testimony here, questions that concern the subject matter -- subject matters that were covered in your written statement, would your answers reflect what's in the written statement and in the list of changes that are on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I hope they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honour, I would now ask that documents P0618 [sic] and P06207 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Documents P06198 and P06207 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Apparently there are associated exhibits to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There are, actually, Your Honour, and I had noticed the Trial Chamber about this through the Trial Chamber's Legal Officer. There are six documents which the witness discussed in the -- in his statement which I would move to have admitted into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those associated documents will form part of Exhibit 770.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Should I -- do I need to refer to them now, because I'm not tendering all of the exhibits that are referred to in the statement, just six specific exhibits which we consider relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently then, you shouldn't refer to them now. Tender them as and when you tender them. So at this stage we'll accepted statements only, because we are not going to -- at this stage, if we accept everything -- if we accept anything that is an annex, it will have to be everything that is annexed, but if you are not going to tender everything that is annexed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- then tender each one of them as and when it becomes relevant to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. So then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So for now we've admitted the statements and the statements only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, if I could have just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have two, and be quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P02345.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see a handwritten comment -- on the document in front of you, sir, do you see a handwritten comment under the letters "KOO"?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know who made that particular comment?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us who that would be?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then there's a comment on the right -- upper right-hand side of the document. Do you know who made that particular comment?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us who made that particular comment?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Osman Vlajcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now what did the -- I'm going to go back to the other comment. What do the letters "KOO" stand for, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: "Counter-intelligence Department."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And in that comment, there's a -- there's the abbreviation "PI." Can you tell us what that stands for, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation "PI" stands for "travel document," "passport."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask now if the usher could help the witness. I just would like him to circle the two comments in different colours so we know who made these comments down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would just ask: First, Mr. Spahic, could you circle the comment that you have identified was made by Mr. Alihodzic with a --

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if you could use a different-coloured pen to circle -- sir, if you could now circle the -- and let the record show that the witness circled the comment about Mr. Alihodzic with a red pen. Sir, now if you could circle the comment made by Mr. Vlajcic?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And let the record show that the witness circled the comment of Mr. Vlajcic with a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I just refer you to the number on this document. And if we could get the English version of the document up on the screen. Oh, we have to save this. Okay. Well, sir, if you could just remember the number "01/1-750", which is the document number of this, and I would now ask that this particular exhibit be captured as an exhibit and be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02345 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 771.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P02384.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, is there a relation between this document, sir, and the document that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: This document refers back to the previous document we looked at, 01/1-750.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would just note for the record that the English translation appears to have the wrong date. It refers to "11/08/1994" whereas the B/C/S version is "11/08/1995". If we could get the whole document on the screen on the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I see the initials "SS" under the textual portion of the document. To whom do those initials belong, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: They are mine, the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why do your initials appear on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Because I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why did you prepare this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I wrote this document on the orders of my superior, specifically Ekrem Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom was this -- or to which entity was this document sent, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: It was sent to the Command of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 772.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P02144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to P02144, Mr. Menon --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Exhibit 771.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- at this stage what is admitted into evidence is just that page that is annotated. I don't know whether you intended to tender the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't really sure of the technical aspects of it, but my intention was to tender the annotated version with the accompanying English translation, which obviously had not been annotated. I was under the assumption that that would be technically possible, but apparently it's not, so I would simply, then, ask that the exhibit be -- that the unannotated version also be admitted into evidence, with the accompanying English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The unannotated version, together with the accompanying English version, are admitted into evidence, that is, of document P02345. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now Mr. Menon has asked for P02144 to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And I just note for the record that this document is dated the 1st of July, 1995. And if we could go to page 2 of the English version of this document, and stay on page 1 of the Bosnian version, but just scroll down on the Bosnian version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the initials "SS" at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom do those initials belong, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: These initials belong to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why do your initials appear on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: They appear because I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And whose signature appears on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could get the whole English page on the screen instead of just the excerpt of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, there's a -- there's a portion of the document that's underlined, actually, and the sentence that follows the underlined part, which reads: "On this occasion, members of the El Mujahid were saying that the basic objective of their struggle was to exterminate the Serbs and Croats ..." As the drafter of this document, sir, can you tell us how you would have come into that -- how you would have come into possession of that particular information?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, you prepared this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could get the English language back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There's a -- do you see the portion of the text which is underlined?

utterances.speaker: SALIH SPAHIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, after that, the sentence which follows that reads: "On this occasion members of the El Mujahid were saying that the basic objective of their struggle was to exterminate the Serbs and Croats ..."
